newsitem.title: UK: FORECAST - Britain's Labour seen stretching lead.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST - Britain's Labour seen stretching lead.

text.p: Britain's opposition Labour party is shaping up to win a 48-seat majority in the coming general election, a Reuters survey of predictions by election experts showed on Wednesday.

Forty-eight seats would be the highest predicted margin for Labour since the survey started last October, up from 43 seats last month and 36 in December, with all but one of the 20 voting experts expecting an end to Conservative rule.
The panel of psephologists and professional market researchers had a growing preference for a late election date, with 16 predicting a May poll, 13 of them specifying May 1.
Under Britain's parliamentary rules, Major must hold the election before May 22.
Although the ruling party has the tactical advantage of deciding the date, some of the experts said that Labour would not be worried about the choice.

"It's in Labour's interests to let them keep going. The longer the Tories carry on, the more it looks like a government clinging to power right to the bitter end," said John Benyon of the University of Leicester.
Reuters asked the experts to predict the number of seats the major parties would win. The overall result is the average of their individual predictions.
David Carlton of Warwick University was once again the only voice on the panel predicting a Conservative victory, for the fifth month in a row tipping a majority of nine seats.
Two contributors were uncontactable this month. Their predictions from last month have been carried forward and are included in the average overall result.

Most panellists saw the Conservative party throwing Prime Minister John Major to the wolves after electoral defeat and four of the 20 marked Health Secretary Stephen Dorrell as his most likely successor.

Deputy Prime Minister Michael Heseltine, Welsh Secretary William Hague and Home Secretary Michael Howard were each tipped from a wide field by two of the experts, while two wagered on Major retaining his hold on the leadership.

"I think the Conservative party after the election will be far more Euro-sceptic and far more rightwing, so I don't think there will be a leader from the left," said Neil Carter, reader in politics at the University of York.
"It's a question of whether they can produce a centrist who can appeal to the right," said Carter, who tipped Major to continue leading the party.

According to the rounded average of 19 predictions for a Labour win, the Conservatives are expected to win 257 seats in the 659-seat House of Commons, compared with 260 tipped a month ago. The Labour party stands to win 351 seats, compared with January's average prediction of 348.
The Liberal Democrats lost one seat from their January tally, with an average prediction of 24 seats in the new parliament. Predicted support for other parties was unchanged from January at 27.
The experts said they expected the general competence of the two parties, in particular their expertise in running the economy, would feature uppermost in people's minds at the time of the election.
The political debate raging over Britain's entry into Europe would not be a major item at the hustings, as the perceived differences between the parties were small, the experts said.
